The list shows how deeply these unseen beings are involved in the spiritual administration of the planet.

L202.t: Nine Racial and Cultural Centers after Adam
rows: The violet race—Adamites and Adamsonites
The second garden and the Adamsonite headquarters near the Kopet mountains
Pre-Sumerians and other Nodites
Near the mouth of the rivers; remnants of the culture of Dalamatia
The Andonites
North and east of the Adamson headquarters, Turkestan, northern Eurasia
The red man
Occupied the Americas, having been driven out of Asia
The yellow race
In control of eastern Asia; advanced settlements bordering on Tibet
The blue race
All over Europe; better centers in the Mediterranean basin and northwestern Europe
Pre-Dravidian India
A complex mixture of races; culture slightly above the outlying regions
The Sahara civilization
Superior elements of the indigo race in what is now the Sahara
The Mediterranean basin
The most highly blended race outside of India
L202.d: Civilization was immensely quickened by the offspring of Adam and Eve, yet thirty-five thousand years ago most of the world still languished in savagery. Paper 78 sketches the racial and cultural distribution of the world before the great expansions of the violet race in nine parts: the violet race in the second garden and the Adamsonite headquarters, the Nodites of Mesopotamia, the Andonites of the north, the red man in the Americas, the yellow race in eastern Asia, the blue man in Europe, the mixed races of India, the indigo peoples of the Sahara, and the blended Mediterranean basin. This survey is the starting point for the story of how the violet race and the Andites spread and transformed world civilization. The hope of the future lay in the second garden between the rivers.

L203.t: Four Factors in the Superiority of the Ancient Yellow Race
rows: Genetic
Largely escaped mixture with debased stocks; northern Chinese benefited by Andite blood
Social
Early learned the value of peace among themselves; first to achieve racial solidarity
Spiritual
Long adherence to the worship of the One Truth proclaimed by Singlangton
Geographic
Protected by mountains to the west and the Pacific to the east; open only in the north
L203.d: From 25,000 to 5000 B.C. the highest mass civilization on Urantia was in central and northern China. The text explains this superiority by four factors. Genetically, the yellow race had largely escaped mixture with debased stocks; socially, they early learned the value of peace among themselves, which increased their numbers and produced racial solidarity. Spiritually, they long adhered to the worship of the One Truth proclaimed by Singlangton; geographically, mountains and sea protected them. The text emphasizes that the stimulus of a progressive and advanced religion is often a decisive factor in cultural development. Notably, the worship of truth as the supreme Deity led to fearless exploration of the laws of nature and the potentials of mankind.

L204.t: Four Factors in the Preservation of Civilization
rows: Conservation of property and wealth
Pooling of the experience of more than one generation
Efficient education of children in the arts and sciences of the past
Development of a strong sense of duty, the enhancement of morality, and the augmentation of ethical sensitivity
L204.d: Ancestor worship played a large part in the long endurance of Chinese civilization. The filial devotion and family loyalty exacted by this growing cult built up superior family relationships and enduring family groups, which in turn facilitated four factors in the preservation of civilization. Property and wealth were conserved rather than scattered; the experience of several generations was pooled; children were efficiently educated in the arts and sciences of the past; and above all a strong sense of duty, morality, and ethical sensitivity was developed. The amazing stability of Chinese culture followed from the paramount position accorded the family. Yet the text also notes the great weakness of ancestor veneration: it promotes a backward-looking philosophy, whereas truth is relative and expanding and lives always in the present.

L205.t: The Three White Races of Europe
rows: The northern white race (Nordic)
The blue man plus the Andite, with Andonite and some red and yellow Sangik
The central white race
Strains of blue, yellow, and Andite, but predominantly Andonite; broad-headed
The southern white race (Mediterranean)
A blend of the Andite and the blue man; secondary Sangik through the Saharans
L205.d: Toward the close of the Andite migrations the racial blends of Europe became generalized into three white races. The northern white race, the so-called Nordic, consisted primarily of the blue man and the Andite with Andonite and some red and yellow Sangik blood, its largest inheritance being from the blue man. The central white race, predominantly Andonite, broad-headed and stocky, is driven like a wedge between the Nordic and Mediterranean races. The southern white race blended the Andite and the blue man and absorbed secondary Sangik blood through the Saharans. The text shows that no race is pure and that the peoples of Europe today are the result of long migration and mixture. The history of blending matters more than any claim of separate descent.

L206.t: The First Four Great Advances in Human Civilization
rows: The taming of fire
The domestication of animals
The enslavement of captives
Private property
L206.d: People today have some spare time to think about society and civilization, but early ancestors had little or no leisure for thoughtful reflection. The text names the first four great advances in human civilization: the taming of fire, the domestication of animals, the enslavement of captives, and private property. Fire, the first great discovery, eventually unlocked the doors of the scientific world, and domesticated animals became living tools that prepared the way for agriculture and transportation. Slavery and private ownership of land came with agriculture; slavery raised the master's standard of living and provided more leisure for social culture. The list shows that civilization grew step by step out of the necessities of survival rather than from ideals.

L207.t: Five Distinct Types of Skeletal Structure
rows: Andonic
Urantia aborigines
Primary Sangik
Red, yellow, and blue
Secondary Sangik
Orange, green, and indigo
Nodites
Descendants of the Dalamatians
Adamites
The violet race
L207.d: Skull dimensions are serviceable in deciphering racial origins, but the skeleton as a whole is far more dependable. In the early development of the Urantia races there were originally five distinct types of skeletal structure: the Andonic aborigines, the primary Sangik red, yellow, and blue, the secondary Sangik orange, green, and indigo, the Nodites descended from the Dalamatians, and the Adamites of the violet race. The first three are evolutionary races; the last two derive from the staff of the Planetary Prince and from the Material Son and Daughter. These five groups later intermingled extensively, and the Lapps and Eskimos come nearest to preserving the aboriginal Andonic type. The list summarizes the history of human origins as written in the body itself.

L208.t: Three Classes of Mankind by Skeletal Structure
rows: The Caucasoid
The Andite blend of Nodite and Adamic stocks; Occidental whites, some Indian and Turanian peoples
The Mongoloid
The primary Sangik type, red, yellow, and blue; Chinese and Amerinds
The Negroid
The secondary Sangik type, orange, green, and indigo; best illustrated by the Negro
L208.d: The five original skeletal types have so intermingled over the last twenty thousand years that they can no longer be clearly distinguished in unearthed remains. Instead, the study of skeletal structures discloses that mankind is now divided into approximately three classes. The Caucasoid is the Andite blend of Nodite and Adamic stocks, further modified by Sangik and Andonic mixture, unified by its proportion of Andite inheritance. The Mongoloid is the primary Sangik type of the red, yellow, and blue races; the Negroid is the secondary Sangik type of the orange, green, and indigo races. Through this list the revelation shows that the familiar threefold racial classification actually grew out of older and more complex origins.

rows: Natural circumstances
Capital goods
Scientific knowledge
Human resources
Effectiveness of material resources
Effectiveness of language
Effectiveness of mechanical devices
Character of torchbearers
The racial ideals
Co-ordination of specialists
Place-finding devices
The willingness to co-operate
Effective and wise leadership
Social changes
The prevention of transitional breakdown
L209.d: Since the Andites have gone forth, there exist no new sources of culture to invigorate civilization, so the civilization now evolving must be maintained and fostered. Paper 81 names fifteen factors on which it is predicated. They begin with material foundations, natural circumstances, capital goods, scientific knowledge, and human resources, and proceed to the effectiveness with which resources, language, and machines are used. Then come the torchbearers who pass on culture through home and school, the ideals of a generation, the co-ordination of specialists and place-finding devices, and the willingness to co-operate, culminating in wise leadership, social change, and the prevention of transitional breakdown. The text adds that civilization is never really jeopardized until able leadership begins to vanish.

L210.t: Two Things Indicated by the Regulation of Sex in Marriage
rows: The relative progress of civilization
Sex gratified in useful channels and in accordance with the mores
The amount of Andite stock in any people
Sex expressive of both the highest and the lowest in physical and emotional natures
L210.d: Paper 82, on the evolution of marriage, examines how the sex urge has been regulated. The regulation of sex in relation to marriage indicates two things. The first is the relative progress of civilization, which has increasingly demanded that sex be gratified in useful channels and in accordance with the mores. The second is the amount of Andite stock in a people; among such groups sex has become expressive of both the highest and the lowest in both the physical and emotional natures. The unmixed Sangik races, by contrast, displayed little imagination or appreciation of the beauty of the opposite sex and posed few problems requiring social control. The regulation of sex thus mirrors both the level of civilization and the inheritance of a people.

L211.t: Two Directions in Which Marriage Functions
rows: In the regulation of personal sex relations
In the regulation of descent, inheritance, succession, and social order—its older and original function
L211.d: Marriage is society's mechanism designed to regulate and control the many human relations arising out of the physical fact of bisexuality. As an institution it functions in two directions: in the regulation of personal sex relations, and in the regulation of descent, inheritance, succession, and social order. We tend to think of marriage first as a matter of personal love and sex, but the text makes clear that the social function is the older and original one. It goes on to say that marriages are hardly made in heaven; the human family is an evolutionary development, and marriage is an institution of society, not a department of the church. Religion should mightily influence marriage but should not undertake exclusively to control and regulate it.

L212.t: Four Sorts of Wives Recognized by Polygyny
rows: The ceremonial or legal wives
Wives of affection and permission
Concubines, contractual wives
Slave wives
L212.d: The institution of polygyny recognized, at various times, four sorts of wives: the ceremonial or legal wives, wives of affection and permission, concubines or contractual wives, and slave wives. The distinction shows that the wives were never equal. The text notes that true polygyny, with all wives and all children of equal status, has been very rare. Usually the home was dominated by the head wife, the status companion; she alone had the ritual wedding ceremony, and only her children could inherit unless by special arrangement. The list reveals that the custom of plural wives actually rested on a hierarchy of property and status, and it helps us understand the long road by which marriage moved beyond that hierarchy toward monogamous pair partnership.

L213.t: Four New Mores Emerging to Stabilize the Marriage-Home Institution
rows: The new role of religion
Parental experience is essential; procreating cosmic citizens—giving sons to the Father
The new role of science
Procreation becoming more and more voluntary, subject to man's control
The new function of pleasure lures
A new factor in racial survival; moderns refuse to bear undesired children
The enhancement of parental instinct
Eliminating from the reproductive stream those whose parental instinct is insufficient
L213.d: Formerly man protected woman because she was his chattel, and she obeyed for the same reason; whatever its merits, that system provided stability. Now that marriage is passing out of the property stage into the personal era, four new mores are emerging to stabilize the marriage-home institution. Religion teaches that parental experience is essential and that procreation means producing cosmic citizens, giving sons to the Father. Science makes procreation voluntary, and pleasure lures lead moderns to refuse to bear undesired children. As a result those with strong parental instinct leave offspring, and parental instinct is enhanced in each generation. The stability of marriage now depends less on outward compulsion and more on inner motivation.

L214.t: Seven Reasons Many Children Were Desired
rows: They were valuable as laborers
They were old-age insurance
Daughters were salable
Family pride required extension of name
Sons afforded protection and defense
Ghost fear produced a dread of being alone
Certain religions required offspring
L214.d: The large families of ancient peoples were not necessarily affectional. The text gives seven reasons why many children were desired. Children were valuable as laborers and served as old-age insurance; daughters were salable. Family pride required the extension of the name, and sons afforded protection and defense. Ghost fear produced a dread of being alone, and certain religions required offspring. Ancestor worshipers regarded the failure to have sons, who would officiate at post-mortem feasts and offer sacrifices, as the supreme calamity for all time and eternity. Notice that nearly all these motives are economic, social, or superstitious. In contrast, the text observes that animals love their children, but civilized man loves his children's children.

L215.t: Three Modern Problems of Child Culture
rows: The large degree of race mixture
Artificial and superficial education
Inability of the child to gain culture by imitating parents—the parents are absent so much of the time
L215.d: Eskimo children, and those of the red and yellow men, thrive on little discipline because they are naturally docile. But children of races with Andite inheritance are more imaginative and adventurous and require more training and discipline. The text names three factors that render modern child culture increasingly difficult: the large degree of race mixture, artificial and superficial education, and the inability of the child to gain culture by imitating parents who are absent from the family picture so much of the time. It goes on to say that bringing a child into the world, instead of conferring parental rights, entails the supreme responsibility of human existence, and warns that any attempt to shift parental responsibility to state or church will prove suicidal to civilization.

L216.t: Four Ways the Soul Could Leave the Body
rows: Ordinary and transient fainting
Sleeping, natural dreaming
Coma and unconsciousness associated with disease and accidents
Death, permanent departure
L216.d: Primitive man thought of the soul as related to the body as the perfume to the flower, and so he believed it could leave the body in various ways: ordinary and transient fainting, sleeping and natural dreaming, coma and unconsciousness from disease and accidents, and death, the permanent departure. In the first three the soul returned; in death it did not. The soul was early man's dream double, and sleep was regarded as proving that the ghost soul could be absent from the body. The text adds that the savage regarded sneezing as an abortive attempt of the soul to escape, which is why sneezing came to be accompanied by such expressions as "⟦Q 86:5.9⟧God bless you⟦/Q⟧!" Traces of primitive soul concepts still linger in modern habits.

L217.t: A New and Expanded World Philosophy of the Spirit Cult
rows: Duty
Those things which must be done to keep the spirits favorably disposed, at least neutral
Right
The correct conduct and ceremonies designed to win the spirits actively to one's interests
Truth
The correct understanding of, and attitude toward, spirits, and hence toward life and death
L217.d: Under the spirit cult, life was at best a gamble; one's future was thought to depend not on effort, industry, or talent but on spirit control. Men studied the will of the spirits by omens, oracles, and divination, and sought to placate them by disguised bribery. Out of this grew a new and expanded world philosophy of three elements: duty, right, and truth. Duty was what must be done to keep the spirits favorably disposed; right was the correct conduct and ceremony to win them to one's interests; truth was the correct understanding of spirits, and hence of life and death. It is striking that key concepts of later ethics began in this primitive dealing with spirits. Even within superstition, the seeds of moral ideas were growing.

rows: Cutting off the head and tying up the body in the grave
Stoning the death house
Castration or breaking the legs of the corpse
Burying under stones, one origin of the modern tombstone
Cremation, a later-day invention to prevent ghost trouble
Casting the body into the sea
Exposure of the body to be eaten by wild animals
L218.d: Man's first efforts at defense were directed not against beasts or enemies but against ghosts. As the ages passed, the living devised many techniques for resisting the dead: cutting off the head and tying up the body, stoning the death house, breaking the legs of the corpse, burying under stones, cremation, casting the body into the sea, and exposing it to wild animals. All were attempts to keep ghosts from returning to trouble the living. The text points out that burying under stones is one origin of the modern tombstone, and that cremation too was invented to prevent ghost trouble. It adds that belief in noise and water as protections against ghosts survives in wakes and holy water. Ancient ghost fear still permeates funeral customs today.

L219.t: Two Objects of Magic, Sorcery, and Necromancy
rows: To secure insight into the future
Favorably to influence environment
L219.d: Civilized man attacks the problems of a real environment through science, but savage man tried to solve the real problems of an illusory ghost environment by magic. Magic was the art of obtaining voluntary spirit co-operation and of coercing involuntary spirit aid through fetishes or more powerful spirits. The text sums up the object of magic, sorcery, and necromancy as twofold: to secure insight into the future, and favorably to influence environment. Remarkably, it says the objects of science are identical with those of magic. Mankind progresses from magic to science not by meditation and reason but through long and painful experience, backing into the truth, beginning in error, progressing in error, and finally attaining the threshold of truth. Only with the scientific method has man faced forward.

L220.t: Seven Influences in the Disappearance of Cannibalism
rows: A communal ceremony assuming collective responsibility for the death penalty
Very early a religious ritual
Only parts or organs supposed to contain the soul were eaten
Limited to men
Limited to the chiefs, priests, and shamans
Taboo among the higher tribes
Human sacrifice sounded the death knell of cannibalism
L220.d: Cannibalism was once widespread among the evolving races, but it gradually disappeared under seven influences. It first became a communal ceremony in which all shared responsibility for the death penalty, and very early a religious ritual. Then only parts believed to contain the soul were eaten; it was limited to men, and next to chiefs, priests, and shamans. It then became taboo among the higher tribes, a taboo that originated in Dalamatia and slowly spread over the world. Finally, human flesh was reserved for the still more superior spirits, and human sacrifice put a stop to man-eating. The list shows that an evil practice was not abolished all at once but overcome in stages, its scope narrowing step by step.

rows: Ghosts—direct spirit influences
Spirits caused disease by enticing the soul out of the body
Violence—obvious causes
War, animal combat, and other readily identifiable agencies
Magic—the influence of enemies
Bewitchment, the evil eye and the magic pointing bow
Sin—punishment for taboo violation
Sickness is a punishment for sin, personal or racial
Natural causation
All disease is the result of natural causes
L221.d: The primitive mind may lack facts, but it is for all that logical. Observing disease and death, thoughtful men sought their causes, and shamans and scientists propounded five theories of affliction according to their understanding. The earliest held that ghosts caused disease by enticing the soul out of the body; then came obvious violence, the magic of enemies, and punishment for taboo violation. Only last was natural causation recognized, and the text notes that the ancient Greeks, having preserved the traditions of Adamson's teachings, were among the first to see that all disease results from natural causes. The progression of causes from spirits to persons to nature epitomizes mankind's slow journey from superstition to science.

L222.t: Seven Tests of Strange Religious Experiences
cols: Test: does it cause an individual
rows: To enjoy better and more complete physical health
To function more efficiently and practically in his mental life
More fully and joyfully to socialize his religious experience
More completely to spiritualize his day-by-day living
To enhance his love for, and appreciation of, truth, beauty, and goodness
To conserve currently recognized social, moral, ethical, and spiritual values
To increase his spiritual insight—God-consciousness
L222.d: Strange religious experiences such as mysticism, ecstasy, and inspiration are not to be judged by their intensity; unrestrained mystical enthusiasm and rampant religious ecstasy are not the credentials of divine inspiration. The text offers a practical test of seven points by observing the fruits of such experiences in the individual. Does he enjoy better physical health, function more efficiently in his mental life, and more joyfully socialize his religious experience? Does his daily living become more spiritual while he faithfully discharges his routine duties? Does his love of truth, beauty, and goodness grow, are recognized values conserved, and is God-consciousness increased? Genuine spiritual experience makes a person whole and leads him toward others rather than into isolation.

rows: Sincerely and courageously facing the problems of universe reality—cosmic stamina
Honestly exhausting the human capacity for human adjustment—industry
Surrendering every wish of mind and craving of soul to spiritual growth
A wholehearted choice of the divine will—obliterating indecision
An unqualified consecration and dynamic dedication to the actual doing of the Father's will
Prayer directed exclusively for divine wisdom to solve specific human problems
Faith—living faith
L223.d: Paper 91, on the evolution of prayer, closes with seven laws of prevailing petitions. The one who prays must first face the problems of universe reality courageously and honestly exhaust the human capacity for adjustment. He must surrender every wish of mind to spiritual growth, make a wholehearted choice of the divine will, and dedicate himself to actually doing the Father's will. His prayer should be directed exclusively for divine wisdom to solve the specific problems met in the Paradise ascension, and finally he must have living faith. The list makes clear that prayer is not a gamble that substitutes for effort, but the act of one who has done his utmost and now aligns himself with the will of God. The power of prayer depends on the attitude of the one who prays.

rows: The adjutant of worship
Superanimal potentials for reality perception—the primordial human instinct for Deity
The adjutant of wisdom
The tendency to direct adoration in higher channels and toward ever-expanding concepts of Deity
The Holy Spirit
The initial supermind bestowal, appearing in all bona fide human personalities
L224.d: Man possessed a religion of natural origin long before any systematic revelation came to Urantia, yet even this evolutionary religion was not his own invention but the product of superanimal endowments. The text names three divine ministries through which it arose. The adjutant of worship awakens the primordial instinct for Deity; the adjutant of wisdom directs that worship toward higher expression and ever-expanding concepts of Deity. The Holy Spirit, the initial supermind bestowal in every bona fide human personality, creates the capacity to realize the postulate of survival. These three are sufficient to initiate the growth of religion, which is later accelerated by Thought Adjusters, seraphim, and the Spirit of Truth. Even the most primitive religion was attended by ministry from above.

rows: The Dalamatian teachings
The First Source and Center first promulgated by Caligastia's one hundred corporeal staff
The Edenic teachings
Adam and Eve again portrayed the concept of the Father of all
Melchizedek of Salem
The third revelation of truth; cardinal precepts were trust and faith
Jesus of Nazareth
God as the Universal Father for the fourth time; essence was love and service
The Urantia Papers
A composite presentation by many beings; the most recent presentation of truth
L225.d: There have been many events of religious revelation, but only five of epochal significance: the Dalamatian teachings of the Prince's staff, the Edenic teachings of Adam and Eve, Melchizedek of Salem, Jesus of Nazareth, and the Urantia Papers. The first two were cut short by rebellion and default, though some of their truths survived through Van and the Sethite priests. Melchizedek made trust and faith the heart of his teaching; Jesus, love and service. The fifth revelation, these papers, differs from all before it in being a composite presentation by many beings rather than the work of a single personality. The text adds that no revelation short of the attainment of the Universal Father can ever be complete; every revelation is partial and adapted to its age.

L226.t: Three Elements Blended in the God Concept
rows: The pre-existent ideas of the evolutionary cults
The sublime ideals of revealed religion
The personal viewpoints of the great religious leaders, the prophets and teachers of mankind
L226.d: In evolutionary religion the gods are conceived in the likeness of man; in revelatory religion men are taught that they are God's sons, fashioned in the finite image of divinity. The God concept people actually hold is a synthesis of the two, blending three elements: the pre-existent ideas of the evolutionary cults, the sublime ideals of revealed religion, and the personal viewpoints of the great religious leaders. The text dwells on the third. Most great religious epochs were inaugurated by an outstanding personality, and men have tended to venerate the leader even at the expense of his teachings. Yet these teachers were the personality fulcrums on which the levers of revealed truth depended. The list reminds us that no God concept is formed by pure revelation alone.

L227.t: Seven Major Religious Epochs of Post-Adamic Urantia
rows: The Sethite period
Sethite priests regenerated under Amosad; never entirely lost the Trinity concept
Era of the Melchizedek missionaries
Proclaimed faith as the price of favor with God
The post-Melchizedek era
Amenemope, Ikhnaton, and Moses, who taught monotheism
The sixth century before Christ
Gautama, Confucius, Lao-tse, Zoroaster, and the Jainist teachers
The first century after Christ
Jesus of Nazareth, Paul of Tarsus, and Philo of Alexandria
The sixth century after Christ
Mohammed founded a religion superior to many creeds of his time
The fifteenth century after Christ
Disruption of Christian unity in the Occident; Sikhism synthesized by Nanak
L227.d: There have been hundreds upon hundreds of religious leaders in Urantia's million-year history, from Onagar to Guru Nanak, and the tide of religious truth has ebbed and flowed many times. The text groups the teachers of recent times into seven major epochs since Adam: the Sethite priests, the Melchizedek missionaries, the post-Melchizedek era of Moses, the sixth century before Christ with Gautama, Confucius, and Lao-tse, the first century with Jesus, Paul, and Philo, the sixth century of Mohammed, and the fifteenth century of Christian disruption and Sikhism. Each renaissance is identified with the life and teachings of some leader. The text closes with the hope that future teachers will strengthen not interreligious barriers but the brotherhood of spiritual worship among followers of differing theologies.

rows: Hinduism—the most ancient
The Hebrew religion
Buddhism
The Confucian teachings
The Taoist beliefs
Zoroastrianism
Shinto
Jainism
Christianity
Islam
Sikhism—the most recent
L228.d: On Urantia, evolutionary and revelatory religion progress side by side, blending into the diversified theologic systems found in the world when these papers were indited. The text enumerates eleven religions of the twentieth century, from Hinduism, the most ancient, through the Hebrew religion, Buddhism, the Confucian teachings, the Taoist beliefs, Zoroastrianism, Shinto, Jainism, Christianity, and Islam, to Sikhism, the most recent. The most advanced religions of ancient times were Judaism and Hinduism, which shaped religious development in Occident and Orient. The great international, interracial faiths are the Hebraic, Buddhist, Christian, and Islamic. The text calls the religions of the twentieth century an interesting study of the social evolution of man's worship impulse.

L229.t: Four Indicators of the Quality of a Religion
rows: Level of values
Loyalties
Depth of meanings
The sensitization of the individual to the idealistic appreciation of these highest values
Consecration intensity
The degree of devotion to these divine values
The unfettered progress of the personality
Realization of sonship with God and never-ending progressive citizenship in the universe
L229.d: Primitive religion was largely a material-value consciousness, but civilization elevates religious values, for true religion is the devotion of the self to the service of meaningful and supreme values. The text indicates the quality of a religion by four measures: the level of its values, revealed in its loyalties; the depth of meanings, the individual's sensitivity to these highest values; consecration intensity, the degree of devotion to them; and the unfettered progress of the personality toward sonship with God and never-ending citizenship in the universe. These criteria matter because they judge a religion not by the correctness of its doctrine or ritual but by the fruits it bears in personality. Every religion may be measured by the same standard.

L230.t: The Seven Commandments of the Salem Religion
rows: You shall not serve any God but the Most High Creator of heaven and earth
You shall not doubt that faith is the only requirement for eternal salvation
You shall not bear false witness
You shall not kill
You shall not steal
You shall not commit adultery
You shall not show disrespect for your parents and elders
L230.d: The seven commandments promulgated by Machiventa Melchizedek at Salem were patterned after the ancient Dalamatian supreme law and closely resembled the seven commands taught in the first and second Edens. Whoever signed the clay-tablet rolls of the Salem church professed belief in El Elyon, accepted the covenant that God's favor rests on faith rather than sacrifices, and promised to obey these commandments. Their distinctive feature is the second: you shall not doubt that faith is the only requirement for eternal salvation, the heart of the Salem teaching. Yet even so short and simple a creed was too advanced for the men of those days. They simply could not grasp the idea of getting divine favor for nothing, by faith.

L231.t: Four Descending Levels of Deity in Present Hindu Theology
rows: The Brahman
The Absolute, the Infinite One, the IT IS
The Trimurti
The supreme trinity of Hinduism—Brahma, Siva, and Vishnu
Vedic and post-Vedic deities
Agni, Indra, Soma, and others, secondary to the Trimurti
The demigods
Supermen, semigods, heroes, demons, ghosts, evil spirits, sprites, monsters, goblins, and saints
L231.d: Hinduism, the oldest and most cosmopolitan of the world's religions, blended the Vedic rituals with the teachings of the Melchizedek missionaries and has kept changing in response to Buddhism, Jainism, Islam, and Christianity. Present Hindu theology depicts four descending levels of deity and divinity: at the top the Brahman, the Absolute and Infinite One; below it the Trimurti of Brahma, Siva, and Vishnu; then the Vedic and post-Vedic deities; and at the bottom the demigods, heroes, demons, and saints. The text observes that were it not for his close identification with the pantheistic Infinite One, Brahma could constitute the foundation for a concept of the Universal Father. This hierarchy displays Hinduism's remarkable adaptability, ranging from lofty speculation to primitive cult practice.

L232.t: Three Factors in Early or Proto-Taoism
rows: The lingering teachings of Singlangton
Persisted in the concept of Shang-ti, the God of Heaven
The Salem religion
A Most High Creator Deity who bestows his favor in response to man's faith
The Brahman-Absolute concept of the Indian philosophers
Coupled with the desire to escape all evil
L232.d: The Salem missionaries commissioned by Melchizedek passed through Asia and reached China in the middle of the second millennium before Christ, and in direct consequence of their teaching the earliest form of Taoism arose. This proto-Taoism, vastly different from the religion bearing that name today, was a compound of three factors: the lingering teachings of Singlangton in the concept of Shang-ti, the God of Heaven; the Salem religion of a Most High Creator who bestows favor in response to faith; and the Brahman-Absolute concept of the Indian philosophers, coupled with the desire to escape all evil. The text relates that this composite belief spread through the lands of the yellow and brown races, and in Japan was known as Shinto. The gospel of faith from Salem lies at the roots of East Asian religion.

L233.t: The Four Noble Truths of Gautama's Original Gospel
rows: The noble truths of suffering
The origins of suffering
The destruction of suffering
The way to the destruction of suffering
L233.d: Buddhism took origin in a historic person, Gautama, not in a myth. He made no superhuman claims for himself or his teachings, but his disciples early began to call him the enlightened one, the Buddha. His original gospel was based on the four noble truths: the noble truths of suffering, the origins of suffering, the destruction of suffering, and the way to the destruction of suffering. That way is the Eightfold Path, from right views to right contemplation. The text explains that Gautama did not intend to destroy all effort, desire, and affection, but to show mortal man the futility of pinning all hope and aspiration on temporal things. The list faces the problem of suffering squarely and then points the way to deliverance.

L234.t: Five Moral Commandments of Gautama's Preachment
rows: You shall not kill
You shall not steal
You shall not be unchaste
You shall not lie
You shall not drink intoxicating liquors
L234.d: The moral commandments of Gautama's preachment were five: you shall not kill, steal, be unchaste, lie, or drink intoxicating liquors. There were several additional or secondary commandments, whose observance was optional with believers. The first four carry the core morality shared by the seven commands of Dalamatia, the laws of Eden, the commandments of Salem, and the Ten Commandments of Moses. That similar precepts recur across distant ages and lands shows that human morality grew from common roots of revelation and from shared experience. The fifth, the prohibition of intoxicating liquors, reflects the Buddhist concern to keep the mind clear in the pursuit of enlightenment.

L235.t: Three Broad Levels Reached by the Minds of the Buddhists
rows: The Gautama legend
The historic life and teachings of Siddhartha, the prophet prince of India, grew in myth
The many Buddhas
An unlimited and infinite number of Buddhas; anyone could aspire to become one
The Absolute Buddha
All Buddhas but the manifestation of some Absolute Source of all reality
L235.d: For over two thousand years the best minds of Asia have sought the truth of the Absolute. The Buddhist ascent to a high concept of the Absolute was less clearly defined than the evolution of the God concept in Hebrew theology, yet it passed through three broad levels. It began with the Gautama legend, the historic life of the prophet prince Siddhartha growing into myth. Then came the teaching of the many Buddhas, reasoned from the expectation that other teachers of truth had come and would come. As their number approached infinity, the concept was reunified in the Absolute Buddha, of whom all Buddhas are manifestations. The text judges that this concept helped unify philosophy but is not vital to religion; even an anthropomorphic Yahweh is of greater religious value than an infinitely remote Absolute.

L236.t: Deity Titles in the Evolution of Jewish Theology
rows: Yahweh
The god of the southern Palestinian tribes, associated with Mount Horeb, the Sinai volcano
El Elyon
The Most High God of heaven, Melchizedek's doctrine of Deity
El Shaddai
A composite from Amenemope, Ikhnaton's Aton, and Melchizedek's teachings
El
The composite Deity embracing all these evolving ideas of divinity
Elohim
The three-in-one God concept; in the singular, Eloah
Sundry names
The Lord, The Almighty, The Holy One, Adonai, The Lord of Hosts, and others
Jehovah
The completed concept of Yahweh evolved in the long Hebrew experience
L236.d: The Hebrews progressed from polytheism through henotheism to monotheism, but the advance was not an unbroken and continuous development; it suffered many retrogressions, and in any one epoch different groups of Semites held varying ideas of God. Numerous titles were therefore applied to Deity, and the revelator defines them to prevent confusion. The list runs from Yahweh, god of the Sinai volcano, through Melchizedek's El Elyon, the composite El Shaddai, the inclusive El, and the trinitarian Elohim, to the many appellations that arose because the Semites disliked to speak the name of their Deity. Jehovah, a much later term, designates the completed concept of Yahweh. The history of these titles is the history of a growing idea of God.

L237.t: The Three Most Popular Mystery Cults
rows: The Phrygian cult of Cybele and her son Attis
The Egyptian cult of Osiris and his mother Isis
The Iranian cult of the worship of Mithras as the savior and redeemer of sinful mankind
L237.d: When Greek philosophy failed to satisfy the masses, the Levant and the Mediterranean world turned to mystery cults that promised personal salvation. Of these, three became most popular. The Phrygian and Egyptian mysteries taught that a divine son had experienced death and been resurrected by divine power, and that all who were properly initiated would share his divine nature and immortality. The cult of Mithras, savior and redeemer, spread most widely of all. The list matters because the idea of a dying and rising god and of salvation through initiation prepared the soil in which Christianity was received in the Occident, and it also became a channel through which the original teachings of Jesus were colored.

L238.t: Seven Sources of the Christian Religion
rows: The Melchizedek teachings
A basic factor in all religions of Occident and Orient for four thousand years
The Hebraic system
Morality, ethics, theology, and belief in Providence and the supreme Yahweh
The Zoroastrian conception
The struggle between cosmic good and evil
The mystery cults
Especially Mithraism, also the worship of the Great Mother
The historic fact
The human life of Joshua ben Joseph, the glorified Christ
The personal viewpoint of Paul of Tarsus
Mithraism dominated Tarsus during his adolescence
The philosophic thought of the Hellenistic peoples
More in harmony with Paul's version of Christianity than any other
L238.d: Christianity as a Urantian system of belief did not arise from the teachings of Jesus alone; it was compounded of many teachings, influences, beliefs, cults, and personal attitudes. The list begins with the oldest root, the Melchizedek teachings, moves through Hebraic morality and theology, the Zoroastrian struggle of good and evil, and the mystery cults, and arrives at the central historic fact of the life of Jesus. Then come the personal viewpoint of Paul and the philosophy of the Greeks. It is striking that the life of Jesus is only one of the seven. The list underlies the observation that, as it became Occidentalized, Christianity lost much of its universal appeal, and it helps distinguish a religion about Jesus from the religion of Jesus.

L239.t: How Religion Can Be Kept Free from Unholy Secular Alliances
rows: A critically corrective philosophy
Freedom from all social, economic, and political alliances
Creative, comforting, and love-expanding fellowships
Progressive enhancement of spiritual insight and the appreciation of cosmic values
Prevention of fanaticism by the compensations of the scientific mental attitude
L239.d: In times of social reconstruction religion is tempted to ally itself with secular power. The revelator names only five means by which religion can be kept free from such unholy alliances. The first and the last are external correctives: a critical philosophy and the scientific mental attitude guard religion against error and fanaticism. The second is institutional independence, while the third and fourth describe what must grow within religion itself, namely fellowship and spiritual insight. The passage goes on to say that religionists as a group must never concern themselves with anything but religion, though any one of them, as an individual citizen, may lead social reform. The business of religion is not to control institutions but to inspire cosmic loyalty in the individual.

rows: The spiritistic belief (in a providential Deity)
Many religions
The humanistic and idealistic belief
Many philosophies
The mechanistic and naturalistic conceptions
Many sciences
L240.d: Religion is passing through a great transition, and transition is always accompanied by confusion. The revelator traces the lack of tranquillity in the religious world to a struggle among three contending philosophies: the spiritistic belief of many religions in a providential Deity, the humanistic and idealistic belief of many philosophies, and the mechanistic and naturalistic conceptions of many sciences. Each is a partial approach to the reality of the cosmos. The struggle is not to end in the victory of one side; the three must be harmonized by a revelatory presentation of religion, philosophy, and cosmology together. Such a revelation portrays the triune existence of spirit, mind, and energy proceeding from the Paradise Trinity and attaining time-space unification within the Deity of the Supreme.

L241.t: Two Basic Reasons for Believing in a God Who Fosters Human Survival
rows: Human experience
Personal assurance, hope and trust initiated by the indwelling Thought Adjuster
The revelation of truth
By the Spirit of Truth, the bestowal of divine Sons, or the written word
L241.d: Science ends its reason-search in the hypothesis of a First Cause, but religion does not stop until it is sure of a God of salvation. On what, then, does belief in a God who fosters human survival rest? The revelator gives two basic reasons. One comes from within: human experience and personal assurance, the hope and trust somehow registered in the mind and initiated by the indwelling Thought Adjuster. The other comes from above: the revelation of truth, whether through the direct ministry of the Spirit of Truth, the world bestowal of divine Sons, or the written word. Since the contemplation of nature reveals only a God of motion and not a personal God, the grounds of belief lie finally in experience and revelation, which confirm each other.

L242.t: Twelve Ways Genuine Spiritual Faith Reveals Itself
rows: Causes ethics and morals to progress despite adverse animalistic tendencies
Produces a sublime trust in the goodness of God despite crushing defeat
Generates profound courage and confidence despite natural adversity and physical calamity
Exhibits inexplicable poise and sustaining tranquillity despite baffling diseases
Maintains a mysterious poise and composure in the face of the rankest injustice
Maintains a divine trust in ultimate victory despite seemingly blind fate
Persists in the unswerving belief in God despite all contrary demonstrations of logic
Exhibits undaunted faith in the soul's survival despite false science and unsound philosophy
Lives and triumphs irrespective of the crushing overload of modern civilizations
Contributes to the continued survival of altruism in spite of human selfishness
Adheres to a sublime belief in universe unity despite evil and sin
Goes right on worshiping God in spite of anything and everything
L242.d: Through religious faith the soul of man reveals itself and demonstrates the potential divinity of its emerging nature. The revelator describes twelve ways in which genuine spiritual faith, true moral consciousness, shows itself. Every item shares one pattern: an adverse condition comes first, whether animalistic tendencies, disappointment and defeat, disease and suffering, injustice, blind fate, contrary logic, false science, the overload of modern civilization, selfishness, or evil and sin, and faith produces trust, poise, and triumph in spite of it. The list closes with the soul that goes right on worshiping God whatever happens. The revelator then says that these twelve spiritlike performances are the third proof that man has a divine spirit dwelling within him.

L243.t: Five Ways Revelation Transiently Clarifies Knowledge
rows: The reduction of confusion by the authoritative elimination of error
The co-ordination of known or about-to-be-known facts and observations
The restoration of important bits of lost knowledge concerning the distant past
The supplying of information to fill in vital missing gaps in earned knowledge
Presenting cosmic data so as to illuminate the accompanying spiritual teachings
L243.d: Revelation is invariably a spiritual phenomenon, yet the truth it contains may be but relatively inspired. Statements concerning cosmology in particular are never inspired, and revelators are not permitted to anticipate future scientific discovery. Even so, such statements are of immense value in transiently clarifying knowledge, and this list names five ways they do so. They reduce confusion by eliminating error, co-ordinate known facts and observations, restore lost knowledge of the distant past, fill vital gaps in earned knowledge, and above all present cosmic data in a way that illuminates the spiritual teachings of the revelation. The list is also a modest guide from the revelators on how the scientific statements of the Urantia Book itself should be read.

L244.t: Two Phases of the Manifestation of Religion
rows: Evolutionary religion
The experience of primitive worship, a mind derivative
Revealed religion
The universe attitude which is a spirit derivative; assurance of eternal realities
L244.d: Science deals with facts, religion with values, and philosophy endeavors to unite the meanings of both. Within this scheme religion displays two phases of manifestation. Evolutionary religion is the experience of primitive worship, a mind derivative, the outworking of the adjutant endowment that fosters the worship trait in evolving man. Revealed religion is the universe attitude which is a spirit derivative, the assurance of and belief in the conservation of eternal realities, the survival of personality, and the eventual attainment of the cosmic Deity. The revelator adds that it is part of the universe plan that evolutionary religion should sooner or later be spiritually expanded by revelation. Evolutionary religion stresses duty, revealed religion love; they are successive stages rather than rivals.

rows: The material body
The supermaterial phase
The soul or even the indwelling spirit
The human mind
The mechanism for intercommunication between spirit and matter
L245.d: Science and religion both start out with the assumption of certain generally accepted bases for logical deduction. Philosophy, too, must begin by assuming the reality of three things: the material body, the supermaterial phase of the human being, which is the soul or even the indwelling spirit, and the human mind that lies between them. The three correspond to the earlier division of facts for science, values for religion, and meanings for philosophy. Notably, mind is set up as a reality in its own right and is defined as the mechanism for intercommunication and interassociation between spirit and matter. Man is explained neither as body alone nor as spirit alone; the mind that chooses and unifies between them stands at the center of this view of human nature.

L246.t: The Sevenfold Salvation of the Faith of Jesus
rows: From material fetters
The personal realization of sonship with God, who is spirit
From intellectual bondage
Man shall know the truth, and the truth shall set him free
From spiritual blindness
The realization of the fraternity of mortal beings; the service-discovery of spiritual reality
From incompleteness of self
The attainment of the spirit levels; the harmony of Havona and perfection of Paradise
From self
Deliverance from the limitations of self-consciousness through the Supreme mind
From time
An eternal life of unending progression in God-recognition and God-service
From the finite
The perfected oneness with Deity in and through the Supreme
L246.d: The teachings of Jesus constituted the first Urantian religion so fully to co-ordinate knowledge, wisdom, faith, truth, and love as to provide at once temporal tranquillity, intellectual certainty, moral enlightenment, God-consciousness, and assurance of survival. The faith of Jesus pointed the way to finality of human salvation, which the revelator unfolds in seven steps. It begins with salvation from material fetters, intellectual bondage, and spiritual blindness, passes through salvation from incompleteness of self, from self, and from time, and ends with salvation from the finite itself. Salvation here is not limited to forgiveness but is an ascending process reaching the ultimate of universe attainment. Such a sevenfold salvation is the equivalent of the completeness of the ultimate experience of the Universal Father, and all of it is potentially contained in human religious experience.

L247.t: Two Practical Manifestations of the Nature and Function of Religion
rows: The ethical reaction of religion
Projecting moral values outward into the affairs of one's fellows
A spiritualized consciousness of divine reality
A censor of mortal affairs, a form of exalted moral confidence
L247.d: While recognizing that religion is imperfect, the revelator holds that its nature and function show themselves in at least two practical ways. The first faces outward: the spiritual urge and philosophic pressure of religion lead a man to project his estimation of moral values directly into the affairs of his fellows, and this is the ethical reaction of religion. The second faces inward: religion creates in the mind a spiritualized consciousness of divine reality, derived by faith from antecedent concepts of moral values, so that it becomes a censor of mortal affairs and an assurance of the realities of time and eternity. Together they show that ethics and spirituality cannot be separated. Faith becomes the connection between moral consciousness and enduring reality.

L248.t: Four Kinds of Religion on Urantia Today
rows: Natural or evolutionary religion
Supernatural or revelatory religion
Practical or current religion
Varying degrees of the admixture of natural and supernatural religions
Philosophic religions
Man-made or philosophically thought-out theologic doctrines
L248.d: The paper on the reality of religious experience opens by sorting the religions of present-day Urantia into four kinds. The first two are distinguished by origin: natural or evolutionary religion grows up from below, while supernatural or revelatory religion is given from above. The third, practical or current religion, is what people actually believe and practice, a mixture of the two in varying degrees. The fourth comprises philosophic religions, theologic doctrines thought out by reason. The classification is a reminder that pure evolutionary or pure revealed religion is rarely found in actual life. The discussion that follows stresses that the personal spiritual experience lying beneath every religion is more fundamental than any of these outward forms.

L249.t: The Seven Absolutes in Which Total Reality Exists
rows: The Universal Father
The Eternal Son
The Infinite Spirit
The Isle of Paradise
The Deity Absolute
The Universal Absolute
The Unqualified Absolute
L249.d: The paper on the Trinity problem sums up total reality, infinity, as it has been presented in these papers: it exists in seven Absolutes. The first three are the Deity persons of the Paradise Trinity, the fourth is the Isle of Paradise, the pattern of nonpersonal reality, and the last three are the Absolutes of potentiality. Actual and potential, personal and impersonal, stand side by side in a single list. The First Source and Center is personality unqualified in the Son but personality potentialized in the Deity Absolute; he is energy revealed in Paradise-Havona but energy concealed in the Unqualified Absolute. These seven become the basic units for the discussion of the triunities and triodities that follows.

L250.t: The First Triunity — the Personal-Purposive Triunity
rows: The Universal Father
The Eternal Son
The Infinite Spirit
L250.d: With the seven Absolutes the First Source and Center forms seven triunities, and the first is the starting point. It groups the three Deity personalities, the Universal Father, the Eternal Son, and the Infinite Spirit; its members are those of the Paradise Trinity, yet it is not the Trinity itself. The revelator calls it the threefold union of love, mercy, and ministry, a divinely fraternal, creature-loving, fatherly-acting, ascension-fostering association. These are the personality-bestowing, spirit-bestowing, and mind-endowing Gods. It is also the triunity of infinite volition, acting in the eternal present and in the past-present-future flow of time, and it provides the mechanism by which personal Deity becomes self-revelatory to the creatures of the evolving cosmos.

L251.t: The Second Triunity — the Power-Pattern Triunity
rows: The Father-Son
The Paradise Isle
The Conjoint Actor
L251.d: The second triunity is the power-pattern triunity. Whether a tiny ultimaton, a blazing star, or a whirling nebula, even the central or superuniverses, every physical pattern from the smallest to the largest material organization derives from its functioning. Its members are the Father-Son, the Paradise Isle, and the Conjoint Actor. Energy is organized by the agents of the Third Source and Center and fashioned after the pattern of Paradise, yet behind all this stands the presence of the Father-Son. The revelator contrasts the two: love may characterize the divinity of the first triunity, but pattern is the galactic manifestation of the second. A warning accompanies the contrast: contact with the God who is love must never eclipse intelligent recognition of the universe fact of Paradise as pattern.

L252.t: The Third Triunity — the Spirit-Evolutional Triunity
rows: The Universal Father
The Son-Spirit
The Deity Absolute
L252.d: The third triunity is the spirit-evolutional triunity; the entirety of spiritual manifestation has its beginning and end in this association. Its members are the Universal Father, the Son-Spirit, and the Deity Absolute. From spirit potency to Paradise spirit, all spirit finds reality expression in the pure spirit essence of the Father, the active spirit values of the Son-Spirit, and the unlimited spirit potentials of the Deity Absolute. The revelator distinguishes the roles briefly: the Father exists before spirit, the Son-Spirit functions as active creative spirit, and the Deity Absolute exists as all-encompassing spirit, even beyond spirit. The existential values of spirit have their primordial genesis, complete expression, and final destiny in this triunity.
